latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Loss of immune tolerance to cartilage-rich matrix antigens creates a relapsing inflammatory substrate in auricular, nasal, laryngotracheobronchial, articular, ocular, audiovestibular, vascular, and other proteoglycan-rich tissues.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Type II collagen and matrilin immune activity
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Humoral and cellular immune responses against type II collagen, matrilin-1, and related cartilage matrix proteins amplify tissue-selective chondritis.
Inflammatory infiltrates at perichondral and fibrocartilaginous interfaces injure chondrocytes and surrounding matrix, producing painful swelling and cartilage destruction.
Systemic cytokine activity drives fever, malaise, anemia of inflammation, thrombocytosis, high ESR/CRP, and occasionally reactive lymphadenopathy.

Cartilage-selective inflammation of the pinna and nasal bridge produces painful erythematous swelling with lobule sparing, nasal tenderness, recurrent flares, and later cauliflower ear or saddle-nose deformity.
Inflammation of laryngeal, tracheal, and bronchial cartilage causes cough, hoarseness, wheeze, stridor, wall thickening, airway narrowing, and steroid-responsive airway edema.
Repeated chondritis destroys cartilaginous support and produces fixed stenosis, dynamic collapse, hypercapnia, respiratory failure, and sudden airway death risk.
Proteoglycan-rich ocular tissues and inner-ear structures may develop episcleritis, scleritis, keratitis, uveitis, retinopathy, hearing loss, tinnitus, vertigo, or vestibular dysfunction.
Inflammation can involve aortic root, aorta, valves, conduction tissue, or myocardium, causing regurgitation, aneurysm, arrhythmia, heart failure, or vascular events.

Seronegative inflammatory arthritis and costochondral inflammation produce arthralgia, joint swelling, chest wall pain, and reduced mobility without the cartilage-invasive pattern of septic arthritis.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Cartilage-directed immune priming permits recurrent responses against matrix antigens.
Matrix-directed immune responses recruit neutrophils, macrophages, plasma cells, and lymphocytes to perichondral interfaces.
Active chondritis can release cytokines that produce fever and acute-phase laboratory abnormalities.
Auricular and nasal cartilage are common clinically visible targets of RP chondritis.
The same chondritis process can involve laryngeal, tracheal, and bronchial cartilage.
Repeated or severe airway inflammation can leave fixed cartilage damage, stenosis, and malacia.
Ocular and audiovestibular manifestations are part of the proteoglycan-rich tissue spectrum of RP.
RP can involve proteoglycan-rich aortic, valvular, and conduction tissues.
Seronegative arthritis and costochondral pain commonly accompany cartilage-directed flares.
Systemic cytokine activity produces low-grade or high fever and FUO presentations.
Relapsing or persistent fever can be a presenting symptom even before classic chondritis is recognized.
CRP commonly rises during active RP flares.
ESR is often elevated in active systemic inflammation.
Inflammatory leukocytosis can accompany active RP, though infection and steroid exposure must be considered.
IL-6 activity can drive reactive thrombocytosis.
Anemia of inflammation may appear in subacute or chronic RP.
Reactive lymphadenopathy is uncommon but reported in systemic RP FUO presentations.
Painful erythematous pinna swelling is the most common visible RP manifestation.
Cartilage-sparing earlobe anatomy makes lobule sparing a useful pattern when auricular chondritis is active.
Repeated auricular chondritis can leave cartilage loss and deformity.
Nasal bridge cartilage inflammation causes pain, tenderness, swelling, and later deformity.
Destruction of nasal cartilage can produce saddle-nose deformity after acute inflammation settles.
Airway chondritis may present with dry or productive cough.
Laryngeal and cricoarytenoid involvement can cause hoarseness and dysphonia.
Upper airway narrowing can produce stridor, especially during severe laryngeal or tracheal inflammation.
Bronchial wall inflammation and narrowing can mimic asthma with wheezing.
CT may show thickened cartilaginous airway walls, often sparing the posterior membranous wall.
Inflammatory thickening and remodeling narrow the larynx, trachea, or bronchi.
Cartilage destruction causes dynamic airway collapse and fixed malacia.
Malacia and stenosis increase the risk of obstructive airway events.
Severe obstruction or collapse can cause CO2 retention, hypoxemia, apnea, and respiratory failure.
Airway obstruction and respiratory failure are major causes of RP morbidity and mortality.
Airway inflammation may produce dyspnea or respiratory distress.
Severe airway obstruction can lower oxygen saturation.
Alveolar hypoventilation from obstruction or collapse raises PaCO2.
Hypercapnia produces respiratory acidosis.
Nonerosive inflammatory arthritis is a common RP manifestation.
Costochondral inflammation can produce chest wall pain and tenderness.
Episcleritis and scleritis are common ocular inflammatory phenotypes in RP.
Uveitis can occur as part of RP ocular involvement.
Keratitis and peripheral ulcerative keratitis are reported ocular manifestations.
Severe scleritis, keratitis, uveitis, retinopathy, or optic nerve involvement can threaten vision.
Cochlear involvement may produce sensorineural hearing loss.
Audiovestibular inflammation can leave permanent sensorineural hearing loss.
Aortic root and valvular involvement can cause aortic regurgitation.
Aortic inflammation can progress to dilation or aneurysm in a minority of patients.
Aneurysm, valvular failure, arrhythmia, or heart failure can drive late mortality.
Severe cardiovascular involvement can be life-threatening.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Both track acute-phase inflammation but can be discordant.
Fever and CRP often rise together during systemic RP flares.
IL-6-driven inflammation can produce both high CRP and reactive thrombocytosis.
Anemia of inflammation can accompany high ESR.
Lobule sparing is only meaningful when auricular chondritis is present.
Ear and nose cartilage involvement can co-occur but either may be isolated.
Wall inflammation and edema commonly narrow the lumen, while chronic malacia may add fixed damage.
Greater stenosis increases clinically important obstruction risk.
Dynamic collapse and loss of cartilage support can cause hypoventilation and CO2 retention.
Higher PaCO2 lowers pH in respiratory acidosis.
Falling oxygen saturation signals clinically dangerous airway compromise.
Respiratory failure is an immediate pathway to death in severe RP.
Severe ocular inflammation can threaten vision.
Active hearing loss can become persistent when cochlear inflammation is severe or recurrent.
Severe valvular disease can lead to heart failure or surgery-level cardiovascular risk.
Severe cardiovascular complications can drive late mortality.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Bleeding or ulcer risk can make NSAIDs unsafe.

failure_modes: Insufficient for airway, ocular, cardiovascular, or destructive cartilage disease

side_effects.interpretation: NSAIDs can precipitate kidney injury in susceptible patients.

treatments.context_specific_role: Symptom control for mild articular or chest wall inflammatory pain without organ-threatening RP.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Uncontrolled infection reduces net benefit and increases toxicity from steroids.
Diabetes, delirium, psychosis, and frailty raise steroid harm.

failure_modes: Insufficient alone for refractory airway disease
treatments.context_specific_role: Core systemic anti-inflammatory therapy for active auricular, nasal, articular, ocular, systemic, or non-crashing airway RP.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Infection must be actively evaluated and treated when high-dose steroids are used.
Severe airway compromise makes rapid anti-inflammatory effect more valuable.

failure_modes: Fixed airway malacia may not reverse
Infection or frailty may dominate outcome

side_effects.interpretation: Pulse steroids can cause severe hyperglycemia.

treatments.context_specific_role: Rapid anti-inflammatory treatment for airway, severe ocular, cardiovascular, or other organ-threatening RP where active inflammation is still reversible.
Steroid-sparing maintenance for recurrent auricular, nasal, systemic, articular, or non-crashing airway RP.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: TPMT/NUDT15 deficiency or prior severe cytopenia limits azathioprine.

side_effects.interpretation: Thiopurines can cause leukopenia or pancytopenia.

treatments.context_specific_role: Maintenance steroid-sparing immunosuppression for recurrent RP, including cases where methotrexate is unsuitable.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: G6PD deficiency or hemolysis risk limits dapsone.

treatments.context_specific_role: Option for selected mild to moderate relapsing chondritis or mucocutaneous/neutrophilic phenotype when safety context allows.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Severe infection can outweigh benefit of cytotoxic immunosuppression.

failure_modes: Fixed airway damage may not reverse

side_effects.interpretation: Cytotoxic immunosuppression increases serious infection risk.
Cyclophosphamide can cause neutropenia and pancytopenia.

treatments.context_specific_role: Escalation option for severe refractory RP with organ-threatening airway, cardiovascular, ocular, neurologic, or renal involvement.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Latent TB or chronic hepatitis requires screening and prophylaxis before TNF blockade.
TNF inhibitors can worsen advanced heart failure.

side_effects.interpretation: TNF blockade increases serious infection risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Biologic option for refractory inflammatory RP, especially airway disease still driven by active inflammation.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: IL-6 blockade can mask fever/CRP and worsen uncontrolled infection.

failure_modes: Fixed structural airway disease may persist

side_effects.interpretation: IL-6 blockade increases infection risk and can blunt CRP response.

treatments.context_specific_role: Option for refractory systemic inflammatory or airway RP where IL-6-driven activity is prominent.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Mechanical stabilization has more value when malacia/collapse drives obstruction.
Procedures can worsen airway edema, bleeding, granulation, or infection.

push_targets.clinical_rationale: Airway rescue can improve oxygenation when obstruction is relieved.
Improved ventilation can lower CO2 retention.

side_effects.interpretation: Airway procedures can cause edema, granulation, or restenosis.
Tracheostomy or stenting can introduce infection risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Mechanical stabilization or rescue for critical stenosis, collapse, or ventilation failure, paired with anti-inflammatory disease control when active inflammation is present.

age_40_to_70.trajectory_modulation: Typical adult onset range; disease can still occur outside it.

axis_response_modulation.rationale: Frailty and cardiopulmonary reserve worsen consequences of airway obstruction.

female.trajectory_modulation: Some cohorts show female predominance, but sex is not decisive.

male.trajectory_modulation: Male sex does not exclude RP; severe airway presentations occur in men.

present.trajectory_modulation: RP often coexists with autoimmune or inflammatory diseases; competing manifolds should still explain their own axes rather than be folded into RP.

axis_response_modulation.rationale: Comorbid inflammatory disease can raise background acute-phase markers.

present.trajectory_modulation: Cartilage inflammation may occur in VEXAS or myeloid disease contexts; this is an OOD/comorbidity signal, not part of the first-layer RP disease name.

axis_response_modulation.rationale: Myeloid disease can deepen anemia independent of RP inflammation.

present.trajectory_modulation: RP can occur despite transplant immunosuppression, but infection and malignancy mimics become more probable.

axis_response_modulation.rationale: Baseline immunosuppression can blunt inflammatory expression in some patients.
Previous airway damage makes fixed stenosis/malacia more likely at presentation.
Preexisting malacia raises risk from a new airway flare.

present.trajectory_modulation: Infection can trigger or mimic RP flares; microbiology and response pattern should enter as explicit evidence.

axis_response_modulation.rationale: Concurrent infection can raise leukocytosis beyond autoimmune inflammation alone.
Limited cardiopulmonary reserve worsens oxygenation during airway involvement.
Comorbid cardiopulmonary disease worsens outcomes of airway or cardiovascular RP.

supportive_care: Rheumatology-led longitudinal monitoring for relapsing cartilage inflammation, steroid toxicity, and need for steroid-sparing therapy.
ENT evaluation for auricular, nasal, laryngeal, or tracheal symptoms; document lobule sparing, nasal bridge tenderness, hoarseness, stridor, and airway sounds.
Urgent airway assessment with CT neck/chest, dynamic expiratory imaging, flow-volume loops, bronchoscopy only when safe, and anesthesia/ICU planning for severe stenosis or malacia.
Pulse oximetry and arterial or venous blood gas assessment when dyspnea, hypoxemia, somnolence, or suspected CO2 retention is present.
Ophthalmology evaluation for red eye, pain, photophobia, keratitis, scleritis, uveitis, or visual symptoms.
Audiology and vestibular assessment for hearing loss, tinnitus, vertigo, or recurrent otologic symptoms.
Echocardiography and CT/MR angiography when murmur, heart failure, chest pain, pulse deficit, aneurysm concern, or systemic cardiovascular involvement is suspected.
Infection, malignancy, IgG4-related disease, GPA, asthma/COPD, amyloidosis, lymphoma, and VEXAS/hematologic disease evaluation when presentation or labs are atypical.
Vaccination review, latent TB/hepatitis screening, bone protection, glucose monitoring, and infection surveillance before prolonged high-dose immunosuppression.
Airway rescue planning with oxygen, noninvasive or invasive ventilation, tracheostomy, dilation, or stenting when obstruction or collapse threatens ventilation.
